introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0765 Pure Maths With Mechanics 1, June 2019, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL questions; each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D and only one answer must be marked (if more than one answer is marked the score for that question is zero). Mathematical tables (formulae booklets) and calculators are allowed. Section A: Pure Mathematics (questions 1 to 35); Section B: Mechanics (questions 36 to 50). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room.

figures.legende: Figure 1 (Q41): uniform ladder AB resting against a rough vertical wall (B at the top), forces 30 N upwards and 10 N horizontal at A, 25 N horizontal at B pointing away from the wall with an unlabelled vertical force at B, weight 20 N at the middle of the ladder and a load of 15 N near B.

incertitudes: Le sujet est un scan sans couche texte de 6 pages (page de garde + 5 pages de questions), lu page par page en image (filigranes gcerevision.com et annotations manuscrites d'un candidat ignorés : elles ne servent pas de clé). La page de garde indique « ADVANCED LEVEL », « 0765 Math With Mechanics 1 », juin 2019, « One and a half hours », 50 questions numérotées 1 à 50 : le scan est complet.

Question 29 : les options B (q implique p) et D (p non équivalent à q, symbole lu comme une double flèche barrée) sont toutes deux vraies, alors que l'énoncé dit « the only statement ... which is true » : la question est convertie en ouverte ; la réponse visée est q implique p (option B).
Question 34 : les options A et D sont imprimées de façon identique (-1/5 + 2/5 i), et c'est la valeur correcte ; impossible de fixer une clé par lettre : question convertie en ouverte.

Question 44 : la force est imprimée F = (15i + 7k) N, d'où un travail de 150 J qui ne figure pas dans les options ; l'option 171 J correspond à 15i + 7j (coquille probable k pour j). Question convertie en ouverte, réponse visée 171 J.

Question 41 : la figure n'est pas en équilibre horizontal (10 N en A vers le mur contre 25 N en B opposé) ; l'équilibre vertical 30 + F = 20 + 15 donne le frottement au mur F = 5 N, puis mu = 5/25 = 0,2 (option A, l'option C porte une unité N à tort). La flèche verticale en B (frottement) est lue sur la figure, sans valeur imprimée. Question conservée en QCM, à relire par un humain.
Question 4 : fractions des options lues avec effort (2/5, 5/2, 5/3, 3/5) ; la valeur 3/5 est celle du calcul.
Question 35 : les options B et D sont partiellement illisibles (chiffres écrasés) ; leur transcription est approximative, sans effet sur la réponse C (seule option de direction -4i + 3j + 2k).
Question 36 : le vecteur position est lu (4t - 1)i + t^2 j + (15t - t^3)k ; l'option D est lue « 14 m/s » (chiffres flous) et recoupe le calcul sqrt(196) = 14.

Question 37 : les vecteurs position (4i + j), 3j et (3i + 4j) sont lus avec effort (chiffres flous) ; ils sont confirmés par l'option C, qui est la somme des moments 40i + 50j. Les numérateurs des options A et D sont flous (distracteurs, sans effet).
Question 39 : l'énoncé demande la vitesse scalaire (speed) ; l'option A est la vitesse vectorielle ; seule l'option D (10 km/h) est un scalaire correct.
Question 46 : les fractions P(A) = 3/10 et P(A u B) = 4/5 sont lues avec effort (un signe « = » est effacé avant 4/5) ; elles donnent P(B) = 5/7, qui est l'option A.
Question 21 : « nC2 = nC3 » lu avec n en exposant gauche (convention ancienne), donc n = 5.
Question 26 : l'exposant 5 de (2 - 3x)^5 est lu en petits caractères ; avec 5 on obtient -1080 (option A) ; l'exposant 6 ne donnerait aucune option.
Question 8 : « In 2 » et « In 4 » sont lus comme ln 2 et ln 4.
Constantes : g = 10 m/s2 est imposé par les questions 43 et 47 et est utilisé tel quel ; aucune autre constante n'est nécessaire.

Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 29, 34, 44. Q29 : options B et D toutes deux vraies ; Q34 : options A et D identiques ; Q44 : force imprimée 15i + 7k, travail 150 J absent des options.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

If $|x+1|<2$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: $|x+1|<2$ means $-2<x+1<2$, so $-3<x<1$. Option B is the solution set of $|x+1|>2$; option A forgets to subtract $1$ from the bounds. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $x>0$, the value of $x$ for which $\log_4 x+\log_4(6x+10)=1$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Combine the logarithms: $\log_4\big[x(6x+10)\big]=1$, so $x(6x+10)=4^1=4$, i.e. $6x^2+10x-4=0$, i.e. $3x^2+5x-2=0$. Factorise: $(3x-1)(x+2)=0$, so $x=\dfrac13$ or $x=-2$. Since $x>0$ (and $6x+10>0$), only $x=\dfrac13$ is admissible. Check: $\log_4\dfrac13+\log_4 12=\log_4 4=1$. **Answer: B.**
$f(-2)=(-2)^3-2(-2)-1=-8+4-1=-5$. A common slip is to mishandle the signs of $-2x$ and the cube of a negative number. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The tangent of the acute angle between the lines $y=4x-3$ and $y=x-5$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The gradients are $m_1=4$ and $m_2=1$. The angle $\theta$ between the lines satisfies $\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|=\dfrac{3}{1+4}=\dfrac35$, which is positive so $\theta$ is acute. Option C is the reciprocal of the correct value. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The period of the function $f(x)=3\cos 5x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The function $\cos(bx)$ has period $\dfrac{2\pi}{|b|}$; here $b=5$, so the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$. The amplitude factor $3$ does not change the period (option C) and option B inverts the ratio. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac{2x}{(x-3)(x-5)}\equiv$
questions.corrige_markdown: Write $\dfrac{2x}{(x-3)(x-5)}\equiv\dfrac{A}{x-3}+\dfrac{B}{x-5}$, so $2x\equiv A(x-5)+B(x-3)$. Put $x=3$: $6=-2A$, so $A=-3$. Put $x=5$: $10=2B$, so $B=5$. Hence $\dfrac{2x}{(x-3)(x-5)}\equiv-\dfrac{3}{x-3}+\dfrac{5}{x-5}$. Check at $x=0$: left side $0$, right side $1-1=0$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The function $f(x)=x^3+1$ is continuous in the interval $[-2,4]$ and differentiable in the interval $(-2,4)$. The value of the constant $c$, $-2<c<4$, for which $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(4)-f(-2)}{4-(-2)}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: This is the Mean Value Theorem. $f(4)=65$, $f(-2)=-7$, so the slope of the chord is $\dfrac{65-(-7)}{6}=12$. Since $f'(x)=3x^2$, we need $3c^2=12$, so $c=\pm2$. Only $c=2$ lies in the open interval $(-2,4)$ ($c=-2$ is an end point). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An arithmetic progression has first term $\ln 2$ and common difference $\ln 4$. The sum of the first 4 terms of this progression is
questions.corrige_markdown: $S_4=\dfrac42\big[2a+3d\big]=2\big[2\ln2+3\ln4\big]$. Since $\ln4=2\ln2$, this is $2\big[2\ln2+6\ln2\big]=16\ln2$. Option A, $16\ln4=32\ln2$, is twice the correct value. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $x^2+y^2=16x$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Differentiate with respect to $x$: $2x+2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=16$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{16-2x}{2y}=\dfrac{8-x}{y}$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The radius of the circle with equation $x^2+y^2-10x+12y+41=0$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Complete the squares: $(x-5)^2+(y+6)^2=25+36-41=20$. The centre is $(5,-6)$ and $r^2=20$, so $r=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A relationship between $(y-2)$ and $(x-1)$ is given by $(y-2)=ab^{(x-1)}$. With a suitable linear relationship between $(y-2)$ and $(x-1)$, the intercept of the straight line on the axis of $\log_{10}(y-2)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Take $\log_{10}$ of both sides: $\log_{10}(y-2)=\log_{10}a+(x-1)\log_{10}b$. This is a straight line of $\log_{10}(y-2)$ against $(x-1)$, with gradient $\log b$ and intercept (value at $x-1=0$) equal to $\log a$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{-x}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{-x}dx=\Big[-e^{-x}\Big]_0^1=-e^{-1}+e^{0}=1-e^{-1}$ ($\approx0.632$, positive, as the integrand is positive). Option D is the negative of this value. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int e^{\ln x^2}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Because $e^{\ln u}=u$ for $u>0$, $e^{\ln x^2}=x^2$. Hence $\displaystyle\int x^2dx=\dfrac{x^3}{3}+K$. Option A wrongly integrates the exponential. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The range of values of $k$ for which the quadratic equation $x^2+2kx+(k+6)=0$ has real and distinct roots is
questions.corrige_markdown: Distinct real roots require discriminant $>0$: $(2k)^2-4(k+6)>0$, i.e. $4k^2-4k-24>0$, i.e. $k^2-k-6>0$, i.e. $(k-3)(k+2)>0$. This holds outside the roots: $k<-2$ or $k>3$. Options C and D include the equality case, which gives equal roots, not distinct roots. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\cos\theta=\dfrac35$ and $\theta$ is an acute angle, then the exact value of $\sin2\theta$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Since $\theta$ is acute, $\sin\theta=\sqrt{1-\frac9{25}}=\dfrac45$. Then $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta=2\times\dfrac45\times\dfrac35=\dfrac{24}{25}$. Option D is $\sin\theta\cos\theta$, i.e. it forgets the factor $2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A $3\times3$ matrix $\mathbf M$ is given as $\mathbf M=\begin{pmatrix}x&1&x-1\\2&1&0\\1&x&0\end{pmatrix}$. If the determinant of $\mathbf M$ is zero, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Expand along the third column, which has two zeros: $\det\mathbf M=(x-1)\begin{vmatrix}2&1\\1&x\end{vmatrix}=(x-1)(2x-1)=2x^2-3x+1$ (the cofactor sign of position (1,3) is $+$). Setting it to zero gives $2x^2-3x+1=0$, with roots $x=1$ and $x=\tfrac12$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The argument of the complex number $z$, where $z=\dfrac{1+i}{1-i}$, is
questions.corrige_markdown: $z=\dfrac{(1+i)(1+i)}{(1-i)(1+i)}=\dfrac{1+2i-1}{2}=i$. So $z=i$ lies on the positive imaginary axis and $\arg z=\dfrac\pi2$. (Alternatively $\arg(1+i)-\arg(1-i)=\dfrac\pi4+\dfrac\pi4$.) Option A is the argument of the numerator alone. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The point $(3,10)$ is on the graph of the function $f(x)$ and $f'(3)=114$. Given that $x=3$ is a first approximate root of the equation $f(x)=0$, using the Newton-Raphson procedure a value of a second approximation to the root of the equation is
questions.corrige_markdown: Newton-Raphson: $x_2=x_1-\dfrac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)}=3-\dfrac{10}{114}=3-0.0877\ldots=2.9123\ldots\approx2.91$. Options A and D come from adding instead of subtracting; option B is a rounding of $2.9123$ to the wrong decimal ($2.92$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A relation $R$ defined on the set of real numbers is such that $xRy$ and $yRx\Rightarrow x=y$. $R$ is said to be
questions.corrige_markdown: The defining property of an antisymmetric relation is: if $xRy$ and $yRx$ then $x=y$. (For example $\le$ on $\mathbb R$.) A symmetric relation requires $xRy\Rightarrow yRx$; reflexive and transitive have different defining conditions. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $y$ satisfies the differential equation $y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x$. If $y=1$ when $x=0$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Separate the variables: $\displaystyle\int y\,dy=\int x\,dx$, so $\dfrac{y^2}{2}=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+c$. With $y=1$ at $x=0$: $\dfrac12=c$. Hence $y^2=x^2+1$. Check: $y\,y'=x$ with $y=\sqrt{1+x^2}$ gives $y'=x/y$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that ${}^{n}C_2={}^{n}C_3$, the value of the integer $n$ is
Given that $x^2-4x-1\equiv(x+B)^2+C$, the values of the constants $B$ and $C$ respectively are
questions.corrige_markdown: Complete the square: $x^2-4x-1=(x-2)^2-4-1=(x-2)^2-5$. Comparing with $(x+B)^2+C$: $B=-2$, $C=-5$. Check by expanding: $(x-2)^2-5=x^2-4x-1$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two functions $f$ and $g$ are such that $f(x)=\ln x$ and $g(x)=9-x^2$. The domain of the composite function $(f\circ g)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $(f\circ g)(x)=\ln(9-x^2)$, defined only when $9-x^2>0$, i.e. $x^2<9$, i.e. $-3<x<3$. Option D is the set where $9-x^2<0$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to3}\left(\dfrac{x-3}{x^2-2x-3}\right)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Direct substitution gives $\frac00$. Factorise $x^2-2x-3=(x-3)(x+1)$, so for $x\ne3$ the fraction equals $\dfrac1{x+1}$, whose limit as $x\to3$ is $\dfrac14$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac{\cos2x}{\cos x-\sin x}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $\cos2x=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=(\cos x-\sin x)(\cos x+\sin x)$. Cancelling $\cos x-\sin x$ gives $\cos x+\sin x$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The coefficient of $x^3$ in the binomial expansion of $(2-3x)^5$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The term in $x^3$ is $\binom53\,2^{2}(-3x)^3=10\times4\times(-27)\,x^3=-1080\,x^3$. Option B drops the sign of $(-3)^3$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_0^2\dfrac{2x}{1+2x^2}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(1+2x^2)=\dfrac{4x}{1+2x^2}$, we have $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2x}{1+2x^2}dx=\tfrac12\ln(1+2x^2)$. Then $\tfrac12\big[\ln9-\ln1\big]=\tfrac12\ln9=\ln3$. Option A forgets the factor $\tfrac12$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are given as $\mathbf a=\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf b=3\mathbf i+\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$. The vector product $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1&2&1\\3&1&2\end{vmatrix}=(2\cdot2-1\cdot1)\mathbf i-(1\cdot2-1\cdot3)\mathbf j+(1\cdot1-2\cdot3)\mathbf k=3\mathbf i+\mathbf j-5\mathbf k$. Check: dotting with $\mathbf a$ gives $3+2-5=0$. Option A has the wrong sign in the $\mathbf j$ component (a sign error in the middle cofactor). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Statement $p$: $x^2=4$ and statement $q$: $x=2$. The only statement below which is true is

*Options as printed:* A) $p\Rightarrow q$   B) $q\Rightarrow p$   C) $q\Leftrightarrow p$   D) $p\not\Leftrightarrow q$
questions.corrige_markdown:
If $x=2$ then $x^2=4$, so $q\Rightarrow p$ is true. But $x^2=4$ also allows $x=-2$, so $p\Rightarrow q$ is false, and therefore $q\Leftrightarrow p$ is false. The last option, as printed ($p\not\Leftrightarrow q$, that is $p$ is not equivalent to $q$), is also a true statement, which contradicts the wording only; the intended answer is $q\Rightarrow p$.

**Intended answer: B ($q\Rightarrow p$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: There are 6 black cards and 4 red cards on a table. In how many ways can 4 cards be selected from the table if the number of colours in the selection must be equal?
questions.corrige_markdown: The condition on equal numbers of colours means the selection has the same number of black and red cards, so 2 black and 2 red. Number of ways: ${}^6C_2\times{}^4C_2=15\times6=90$. Option A is ${}^6C_2$ alone. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equations of the asymptotes of the graph of the curve $y=\dfrac{x-2}{x^2-4x+3}$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: The denominator factorises as $x^2-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3)$ and the numerator does not vanish at $1$ or $3$, so there are vertical asymptotes $x=1$ and $x=3$. As $x\to\pm\infty$ the numerator has lower degree than the denominator, so $y\to0$: the horizontal asymptote is $y=0$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\sin(x+y)=x$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Differentiate implicitly: $\cos(x+y)\left(1+\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)=1$. So $1+\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac1{\cos(x+y)}$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac1{\cos(x+y)}-1=\dfrac{1-\cos(x+y)}{\cos(x+y)}$. Option D has the opposite sign. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The relationship between two variables $x$ and $y$ is expressed by the values in the table below.

| $x$ | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 0.693 | 1.099 | 1.386 | 1.609 |

Using the trapezium rule, $\displaystyle\int_2^5 y\,dx\approx$
questions.corrige_markdown: The ordinates are equally spaced with $h=1$ (three strips). Trapezium rule: $\dfrac h2\big[y_0+y_3+2(y_1+y_2)\big]=\dfrac12\big[0.693+1.609+2(1.099+1.386)\big]=\dfrac12\big[2.302+4.970\big]=\dfrac{7.272}{2}=3.636$. (The values are $\ln x$, and the exact integral $\int_2^5\ln x\,dx\approx3.6$.) Option D transposes two digits. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
If $z=\dfrac{1+2i}{3-4i}=a+bi$, then $z=$

*Options as printed:* A) $z=-\dfrac15+\dfrac25i$   B) $z=-\dfrac25+\dfrac15i$   C) $z=-\dfrac15-\dfrac25i$   D) $z=-\dfrac15+\dfrac25i$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator: $z=\dfrac{(1+2i)(3+4i)}{(3-4i)(3+4i)}=\dfrac{3+4i+6i+8i^2}{25}=\dfrac{-5+10i}{25}=-\dfrac15+\dfrac25i$. Options A and D are printed identically in the scan and both equal this value, so the key cannot be fixed by letter.

**Intended answer: A ($z=-\dfrac15+\dfrac25i$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The position vectors of the points $A$ and $B$ are $\overrightarrow{OA}=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=-2\mathbf i+4\mathbf j-2\mathbf k$. A vector equation of the line passing through $A$ and $B$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: A line through $A$ with direction $\overrightarrow{AB}$ has equation $\mathbf r=\overrightarrow{OA}+\mu\overrightarrow{AB}$. Here $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}=(-2-2)\mathbf i+(4-1)\mathbf j+(-2+4)\mathbf k=-4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$. So $\mathbf r=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k+\mu(-4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$. Option A has the wrong sign on the $\mathbf i$ component of the direction; options B and D use the direction $2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k$, which is $\overrightarrow{OA}$, not $\overrightarrow{AB}$. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: $\mathbf r=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k+\mu(4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$
$\mathbf r=-4\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k+\mu(2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k)$
$\mathbf r=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k+\mu(-4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$
$\mathbf r=-4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j-2\mathbf k+\mu(2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k)$

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: MECHANICS**

A particle moves so that after $t$ seconds its position vector is $\mathbf r$, where $\mathbf r=\big[(4t-1)\mathbf i+t^2\mathbf j+(15t-t^3)\mathbf k\big]$ m. The speed of the particle after 3 seconds is
questions.corrige_markdown: Velocity $\mathbf v=\dfrac{d\mathbf r}{dt}=4\mathbf i+2t\,\mathbf j+(15-3t^2)\mathbf k$. At $t=3$: $\mathbf v=4\mathbf i+6\mathbf j-12\mathbf k$ $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The speed is the magnitude: $\sqrt{4^2+6^2+(-12)^2}=\sqrt{16+36+144}=\sqrt{196}=14\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Option A is the velocity vector, not the speed (a scalar). Option C is $\sqrt{3^2+6^2+12^2}$. **Answer: D.**

themes: centre of mass of composite bodies
questions.enonce_markdown: Three particles of weight $7\ \mathrm N$, $9\ \mathrm N$ and $4\ \mathrm N$ have position vectors $(4\mathbf i+\mathbf j)\ \mathrm m$, $3\mathbf j\ \mathrm m$ and $(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)\ \mathrm m$ respectively. The position vector of their centre of mass is
questions.corrige_markdown: Weights are proportional to masses, so $\bar{\mathbf r}=\dfrac{\sum w\,\mathbf r}{\sum w}$. Total weight $=7+9+4=20\ \mathrm N$. $\sum w\mathbf r=7(4\mathbf i+\mathbf j)+9(3\mathbf j)+4(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)=(28+12)\mathbf i+(7+27+16)\mathbf j=40\mathbf i+50\mathbf j$. So $\bar{\mathbf r}=\dfrac{40\mathbf i+50\mathbf j}{20}=2\mathbf i+\dfrac52\mathbf j$. Option C is the unnormalised moment sum (forgetting to divide by the total weight). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two fair dice are thrown together. The probability that the product of the scores will be at least 20 is
questions.corrige_markdown: There are $36$ equally likely outcomes. Products $\ge20$: $(4,5),(5,4),(4,6),(6,4),(5,5),(5,6),(6,5),(6,6)$, i.e. $8$ outcomes (products $20,20,24,24,25,30,30,36$; note $3\times6=18<20$). Probability $=\dfrac8{36}=\dfrac29$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A man travelling due East with speed of $8\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ watches a boy cycling along a straight road. The boy appears to be cycling due South with speed of $6\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$. The actual speed of the boy is
questions.corrige_markdown: Take $\mathbf i$ East and $\mathbf j$ North. The man's velocity is $\mathbf v_M=8\mathbf i$. The velocity of the boy relative to the man is $\mathbf v_{B/M}=-6\mathbf j$. Then the boy's actual velocity is $\mathbf v_B=\mathbf v_M+\mathbf v_{B/M}=8\mathbf i-6\mathbf j$, and its speed is $|\mathbf v_B|=\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=10\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$. Option A is the velocity vector, whereas the question asks for the speed; B and C add or subtract the magnitudes. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle moving in a horizontal circle of radius $0.5\ \mathrm m$ has a speed $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The angular speed of the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown: $v=r\omega$, so $\omega=\dfrac vr=\dfrac{12}{0.5}=24\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. Options A and D have the wrong time unit (minutes instead of seconds). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Fig. 1 shows a uniform ladder $AB$ with a load on it. It is leaning against a rough vertical wall. The forces acting on the ladder are as shown.

![fig-1](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

The coefficient of friction between the ladder and the wall is
questions.corrige_markdown: At the wall $B$ the forces are the normal reaction $R=25\ \mathrm N$ (horizontal, away from the wall) and the friction force $F$ (vertical, upwards, drawn at $B$). Take the vertical forces on the ladder: upward $30\ \mathrm N$ (at $A$) $+F$, downward $20\ \mathrm N$ (weight) $+\ 15\ \mathrm N$ (load). Equilibrium: $30+F=20+15$, so $F=5\ \mathrm N$. With friction at the wall, the coefficient is $\mu=\dfrac FR=\dfrac5{25}=0.2$. A coefficient of friction has no unit, so option C ($0.2\ \mathrm N$) is wrong; options B and D would need $F=10\ \mathrm N$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A car of mass $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ travelling along a straight path accelerates uniformly from $15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to $25\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in a distance of $320\ \mathrm m$. The resistance to the motion of the car is $145\ \mathrm N$. The driving force of the engine of the car is
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $v^2=u^2+2as$: $625=225+2a(320)$, so $a=\dfrac{400}{640}=0.625\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Newton's second law along the path (positive in the direction of motion): $D-145=1000\times0.625=625$, so $D=625+145=770\ \mathrm N$. Option A subtracts the resistance instead of adding it ($625-145=480$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle of mass $15\ \mathrm{kg}$ rests on a smooth horizontal table. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table to another particle of mass $10\ \mathrm{kg}$ which hangs freely. Taking $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and given that the acceleration of the system is $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ when the system is released from rest, the force exerted by the string on the pulley is
questions.corrige_markdown: For the particle on the smooth table the only horizontal force is the tension $T$: $T=15\times4=60\ \mathrm N$. (Check with the hanging mass: $10\times10-T=10\times4$ gives $T=60\ \mathrm N$.) The string pulls on the pulley with $60\ \mathrm N$ along the horizontal part and $60\ \mathrm N$ along the vertical part; these are perpendicular, so the resultant is $\sqrt{60^2+60^2}=60\sqrt2\ \mathrm N$. Option C is just the tension. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The work done when the point of application of a force $\mathbf F=(15\mathbf i+7\mathbf k)\ \mathrm N$ moves through a displacement $\mathbf r=(10\mathbf i+3\mathbf j)\ \mathrm m$ is

*Options as printed:* A) $171\ \mathrm J$   B) $21\ \mathrm J$   C) $46\ \mathrm J$   D) $21\ \mathrm{kJ}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Work done $=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf r$. With the force exactly as printed, $\mathbf F=15\mathbf i+7\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf r=10\mathbf i+3\mathbf j$, so $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf r=15\times10+0\times3+7\times0=150\ \mathrm J$, which is not among the options. The option $171\ \mathrm J=150+7\times3$ is what one obtains if the force is $\mathbf F=(15\mathbf i+7\mathbf j)\ \mathrm N$, which is almost certainly the intended question (the scan prints $\mathbf k$, a probable typographical error).

**Intended answer: A ($171\ \mathrm J$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

themes: centre of mass of composite bodies
questions.enonce_markdown: Three particles of masses $5\ \mathrm{kg}$, $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ are placed at the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ whose position vectors are $(\mathbf i+3\mathbf j)\ \mathrm m$, $(7\mathbf i-3\mathbf j)\ \mathrm m$ and $(-3\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)\ \mathrm m$ respectively. The position vector of their centre of mass is
questions.corrige_markdown: Total mass $=5+3+2=10\ \mathrm{kg}$. $\sum m\mathbf r=5(\mathbf i+3\mathbf j)+3(7\mathbf i-3\mathbf j)+2(-3\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)=(5+21-6)\mathbf i+(15-9+4)\mathbf j=20\mathbf i+10\mathbf j$. So $\bar{\mathbf r}=\dfrac{20\mathbf i+10\mathbf j}{10}=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $A$ and $B$ are two independent events such that $P(A)=\dfrac3{10}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac45$, $P(B)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: For independent events $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A)P(B)$. Let $p=P(B)$: $\dfrac45=\dfrac3{10}+p-\dfrac3{10}p=\dfrac3{10}+\dfrac7{10}p$. So $\dfrac7{10}p=\dfrac12$ and $p=\dfrac57$. Check: $\dfrac3{10}+\dfrac57-\dfrac3{10}\cdot\dfrac57=\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{5}{7}-\dfrac{3}{14}=\dfrac{21+50-15}{70}=\dfrac45$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle of mass $M\ \mathrm{kg}$ is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a fixed smooth pulley to a particle of mass $6\ \mathrm{kg}$. Both particles are hanging freely. When the system is released and is moving in the direction of the $6\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass with acceleration $2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, and taking $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the value of $M$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The $6\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass moves down, so for it (positive downwards): $6g-T=6a$; for the mass $M$ (moving up): $T-Mg=Ma$. Adding: $(6-M)g=(6+M)a$, so $(6-M)\times10=(6+M)\times2$, i.e. $60-10M=12+2M$, so $12M=48$ and $M=4\ \mathrm{kg}$. Check: $a=\dfrac{(6-4)\times10}{10}=2$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two bodies of mass $m$ and $4m$ are moving with equal momentum. The ratio of their kinetic energies is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a body of mass $M$ and momentum $p$, $E_k=\dfrac12Mv^2=\dfrac{p^2}{2M}$. With the same $p$: $E_1:E_2=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}:\dfrac{p^2}{8m}=4:1$ (taking the bodies in the order $m$ then $4m$). Option A is the inverse ratio (it would be the answer for $E_{4m}:E_m$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A force $\mathbf F=(2\mathbf i-6\mathbf j-\mathbf k)\ \mathrm N$ displaces a particle on a plane from one point with position vector $\mathbf r=4\mathbf j\ \mathrm m$ to another point with position vector $\mathbf r=(3\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-5\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$. The work done by $\mathbf F$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The displacement is the final minus the initial position: $\mathbf d=(3\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-5\mathbf k)-4\mathbf j=3\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-5\mathbf k$. Work $=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=2(3)+(-6)(-2)+(-1)(-5)=6+12+5=23\ \mathrm J$. Using the final position vector alone gives $6-12+5=-1$, not an option. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A bar $AB$ of length $0.6\ \mathrm m$ and weight $3\ \mathrm N$ is suspended horizontally by two strings at $A$ and $B$. Given that its centre of gravity is $0.4\ \mathrm m$ from $A$, the tension in the string at $A$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Let $T_A$ and $T_B$ be the tensions (vertical). Take moments about $B$: the weight acts $0.6-0.4=0.2\ \mathrm m$ from $B$, so $T_A\times0.6=3\times0.2$ and $T_A=\dfrac{0.6}{0.6}=1.0\ \mathrm N$. Then $T_B=3-1.0=2.0\ \mathrm N$ (check by moments about $A$: $T_B\times0.6=3\times0.4$, $T_B=2.0\ \mathrm N$). **Answer: D.**
